job: Fresh graduate in computing and engineering
name: Iris Tanaka

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hello Iris. I'm a senior field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. What you tell me is confidential, so you can say what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, tell me about a normal day right now.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I get up at six on Saturdays and Sundays for the bakery shift on Brantford Road, and on weekdays I'm in the library at Northfield University with my notebook. I'm doing a master's in water and environmental engineering, mostly because forty-odd job applications for my civil engineering degree went nowhere. I do my calculations by hand first and only then type them up. My room in the student house costs 380 a month and I share a kitchen with five people.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What was your degree, and how did it go?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Civil engineering, a pass, so an average mark. My final project was a footbridge design that I only just got finished, and I had no internship because I was working weekends to pay the rent. My mum drives a city bus and is her depot's union rep. She can't help with money, but she taught me to read a contract before signing it. I owe about thirty-one thousand in loans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The scenario is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's what I expected: a lot of noise and not much change. The chatbot on the university portal still gets my timetable wrong, so I'm not scared of it. Online I'd probably just post that the money would be better spent on real bridges.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, nothing changes for me, and that's the problem. I still have thirty-one thousand in loans and few civil firms hiring near here. Most firms that do hire want two years of experience for a graduate job, and I don't have any.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish the master's, keep the bakery shifts and send out at least five applications every week. I'd also ask my tutor Dr Okafor to introduce me to the water company's graduate scheme. I'd stay away from AI tools; I'd rather learn the actual calculations properly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Tense, honestly. It's not the AI that worries me, it's the loan statement that arrives every spring. I feel like I'm running to stand still.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said firms want experience. Where would a person without internships get it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That's the trap. My mum says the unions used to fix this with proper apprenticeships, and now every firm wants someone else to train people. I'd take an unpaid month on a site if I could afford it, but I can't, because the bakery pays my rent.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What gets cut first if money gets tighter?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The phone contract goes first, then the bus pass, and I'd walk to the library. I wouldn't cut the bakery shifts, but I might add a third one. I need to hold on to this degree year more than I need to hold on to sleep.

say: I'd say AI is mostly **hype** and the money should go to real infrastructure.
I'd tell friends the portal chatbot still gets my timetable wrong.
think: I still carry **thirty-one thousand** in loans and nobody near here is hiring graduates.
The trap is experience: firms want it, and nobody pays me to get it.
do: Finish the **master's** and keep the two weekend bakery shifts.
Send five **applications** a week and ask Dr Okafor (my tutor) about the water company scheme.
Keep doing calculations by hand and stay away from AI tools.
feel: Tense and tired, because the **loan statement** worries me more than any technology.
S0.quote: I still have thirty-one thousand in loans and few civil firms hiring near here.
fieldNote: Her fear is **debt** and the experience trap, not AI itself.
Resistant to tools: she describes doing calculations by hand first and does not trust the chatbot.
Her mother's **union** background shapes who she blames: firms that won't train.

steps.text: Keep both weekend shifts at the bakery on Brantford Road
Put aside 40 a month toward the spring loan payment
Send five applications a week and ask Dr Okafor about the water company scheme

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The scenario is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's the first time my worry feels real. Checking calculations and drawing up plans are exactly the jobs a graduate gets given, and software can do them now. I'd post that firms should be made to keep hiring trainees.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think the entry-level desk work is where it lands first, and that's my door in. The firms near me will keep three engineers instead of five and use software for the rest. I'd be one of the ones who never gets hired, and I'm already near the back of the queue.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd push toward site-based roles with the water company or a contractor, where someone has to stand in a trench and look. I'd go to the union meeting my mum belongs to and ask about a training levy. And I'd have to learn the design software they use, even though I dislike it. I'd do that in the library, not at home.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Angry, more than scared. It's not that I think technology is evil. I'm angry that firms can swap people for software and nobody asks the new graduates.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd learn the software you dislike. What changed your mind?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pride only works when I can pay rent. If the water company wants a graduate who can run their modelling tool, I'd learn the tool for a month and complain the whole time, but I'd still check the output by hand. A wrong pipe size is a real flood.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you worry about most?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The other people in my house on the master's. A few of them are better than me and have no more money than I do. If they struggle to find work, I know where I stand.

say: I'd say software is taking the **checking and drawing** work that graduates need.
I'd demand firms be made to keep hiring **trainees**.
think: Entry-level desk work is where my **first job** would have been, and firms will keep fewer engineers.
I'm near the back of the queue and I know it.
do: Aim for **site-based** roles with the water company or a contractor.
Ask at my mum's union meeting about a **training levy** for new graduates.
Learn the firm's design software in the library for a month, grudgingly.
feel: **Angry** that firms can swap people for software without asking new graduates.
S1.quote: I'd learn the tool for a month and complain the whole time, but I'd still check the output by hand.
fieldNote: Her resistance **bends** under money pressure: she would learn the software but keeps her check-by-hand habit.
Blames firms and wants collective, union-style fixes.
Expects to be among the ones not hired, which is why alarmed rather than anxious.

steps.text: Apply to the water company and contractors for site-based graduate roles
Go to the next union meeting with my mum and ask about a training levy
Spend a month learning the firm's design software in the library
Ask the university careers office for a paid placement

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The scenario is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years is almost nothing. I'd say it out loud: this has to be slowed down, or the government has to step in. I'd say it at the union meeting and at the bakery, and probably on the bus to my mum.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: What I think privately is this. My degree will be done before I've paid for it. I finish the master's in a year, and by then the entry-level engineering jobs are mostly gone. I have no plan for that. I don't have savings, and my mum has none to give.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd probably stop the master's if the loan allowed, but it doesn't, so I'd finish it. I'd ask my mum's union and the council what help there'd be for young people with debt. I'd try for a site job or something hands-on, because I'd have until about 2031 before robots are doing that too. Beyond that, I really don't know.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Cold and a bit sick. The word I keep landing on is panic, because I can't see where I'd stand in two years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you don't know. What would the next month look like?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stop going to the library and sit on the phone to the loan company and the council, trying to find out what happens to my debt. I'd work every shift the bakery would give me. I'd also write to my MP, the first time I'd ever have done it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything in this picture that helps?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only that everyone's in it together. If everyone's graduates are in trouble, then maybe the loans get written off, and a government has to act. But I don't trust that to happen quickly, because they never do anything quickly.

say: I'd say this must be **slowed down** or the government has to step in.
I'd raise it at the union meeting and with the bakery staff.
think: My degree could be **finished before I've paid** for it, with no entry-level jobs left.
I have no savings, and my mum can't help.
do: Finish the **master's** because the loan leaves no choice.
Ask my mum's union and the **council** what help exists for graduates with debt.
Chase **hands-on** site jobs while they last, until about 2031.
feel: **Cold and sick**, because I can't see where I'd stand in two years.
S2.quote: I finish the master's in a year, and by then the entry-level engineering jobs are mostly gone.
fieldNote: Has the least room to move: **debt**, no savings and no family help.
Her only hope is collective political action, but she doesn't trust it to be fast.
Says she has no plan, which fits panicked on the scale.

steps.text: Phone the loan company and council to find out what happens to my debt
Join my mum's union meeting and ask about help for graduates
Write to my MP about slowing AI and protecting graduates
Chase site and hands-on jobs that robots won't reach until around 2031

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The scenario is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years is long enough to get angry and organise. I'd say that we need a plan now, not in 2031 when people are already out of work. I'd say it to anyone who'll listen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be alarmed, but I'd have a chance. If I get a first job by 2028 or so, I'd have a couple of years to build a skill that isn't just desk work. If I don't get one, I'll be starting from nothing. I'd say that's the bit that keeps me awake.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish the master's and then take any site-based or utilities job I could get, even a poorly paid one, to get a foot in. I'd join the union branch and go to meetings. I'd also learn a trade skill on the side, maybe pipe-fitting or surveying, because hands-on work lasts until about 2034.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Better than the two-year one, but not good. Five years is the difference between standing in a flood and seeing the water coming. I'd still be scared, but I could move.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd learn a trade skill. Which one, and who would pay?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably surveying, because it combines my degree with being outside. The water company runs a night course, and my tutor says the fee is under four hundred. I'd pay it from bakery shifts over a few months, even if it meant no holiday.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your mum?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That I'm all right and she shouldn't worry, which would be a lie. She'd see through it in a second, though. Then she'd ask me what the union could do, and she'd have a better answer than I would.

say: I'd say we need a **plan now**, not in 2031 when people are already out of work.
think: If I get a first job by about **2028** I'd have time to build skills; if not, I start from nothing.
do: Finish the master's and take any **site-based or utilities** job, even poorly paid.
Join the union **branch** and go to the meetings.
Pay for a night **surveying** course from bakery shifts, under four hundred.
feel: Better than two years, but still **scared**; I could at least move.
S3.quote: Five years is the difference between standing in a flood and seeing the water coming.
fieldNote: The extra years turn panic into a **plan**: surveying, utilities and union activity.
Still alarmed because her income depends on landing a first job in the next two years.
Her mum remains her emotional anchor.

steps.text: Take any site-based or utilities job offered after the master's
Pay for the night surveying course from bakery shifts
Join the union branch and go to every meeting

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The scenario is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years is a different story. I'd say it's a chance to get ready, and that schools and councils should start funding retraining now. I wouldn't be shouting, I'd be organising.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be anxious, not alarmed. Ten years lets me pay off a chunk of debt and get a few years of real experience first. By 2036 I'd be 34, with a decent track record if I'm lucky. The worry would be that AGI replaces the whole path, not just my first job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish the master's, take a site job and stay in it for at least three years, saving 100 a month. I'd learn a second skill, possibly surveying or drone mapping, and I'd be active in the union. I'd also try to help build a local scheme for training graduates, because I think it matters.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Almost calm on some days. I feel I'd have time to make mistakes, which I don't have today.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said almost calm on some days. What are the other days like?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The days when the loan statement comes, or when a friend loses a contract. Then I think ten years is a long time to worry about it, and not long enough to fix it. But on good days I can imagine a normal life, a flat of my own.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's the one thing you would do differently from today?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start saving a little right away, even if it's only ten a month, so it's a habit. And I'd ask for help earlier. I waited too long to talk to my tutor, which cost me a year.

say: I'd say schools and councils should start funding **retraining** for young graduates now.
I wouldn't be shouting about it, I'd be quietly **organising** through the union.
think: With ten years I could pay off a chunk of debt and build **real experience**.
I worry AGI replaces the whole career path, not just my first job.
do: Take a **site job** and stay three years, saving 100 a month.
Learn a second skill such as **surveying** or drone mapping.
Help start a local graduate **training scheme** through the union.
feel: Almost **calm** on good days, because I'd have time to make mistakes.
S4.quote: Ten years is a long time to worry about it, and not long enough to fix it.
fieldNote: The only scenario where she imagines **ordinary adult life**.
Debt remains the main stress; AGI is a longer-term concern.
Practical and organising rather than fearful.

steps.text: Take a site job and stay in it for three years
Save 100 a month toward the loan and a flat deposit
Learn surveying or drone mapping as a second skill
Help the union branch set up a local graduate training scheme

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one worries me most, because it leaves no time to pay down debt or learn another trade. What would help is a real graduate guarantee, meaning proper paid trainee places and some of the loan written off if the jobs vanish. I'd also want unions and councils to speak up for young engineers, because we don't have the money to speak for ourselves.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Only that people like me aren't lazy and aren't against technology. We're just standing at the start of a ladder when somebody's cutting the bottom rungs. Somebody should ask the graduates before they decide.

headlineQuote: We're just standing at the start of a ladder when somebody's cutting the bottom rungs. Somebody should ask the graduates before they decide.
portrait: Iris is a 24-year-old civil engineering graduate doing a **master's** in water engineering, living in student housing.
She carries about **thirty-one thousand** in loans and works weekend bakery shifts to pay the rent.
Her mother, a bus driver and **union rep**, shapes her view: firms should train graduates, not shed them.
She's wary of AI tools and checks work by hand, but she'd learn software if rent depended on it.
Her mood runs from anxious to **panicked**, easing only when she has ten years to prepare.
biggestWorry: The **two-year** picture worries her most, because there'd be no time to pay down debt or build experience.
whatWouldHelp: A **graduate guarantee**: paid trainee places and part of the loans written off if jobs vanish.
Unions and councils **speaking up** for young engineers.
